title: Book 7, Chapter 21 — Eighteenth and Nineteenth Years of the War—Arrival of Gylippus at Syracuse—Fortification of Decelea—Successes of the Syracusans
paragraphs: After refitting their ships, Gylippus and Pythen coasted from Tarentum to Epizephyrian Locris. They now received better information that Syracuse was not yet completely invested, and that it was still possible for an army arriving at Epipolae to make its way in. They debated whether to keep Sicily on their right and risk sailing in by sea, or, leaving it on their left, to first sail to Himera and, taking with them the Himeraeans and any others who would join, go to Syracuse by land. They finally decided to sail for Himera, especially since the four Athenian ships that Nicias had at last sent off, on hearing they were at Locris, had not yet reached Rhegium. Accordingly, before these ships reached their post, the Peloponnesians crossed the strait, and after touching at Rhegium and Messina came to Himera. On arrival there they persuaded the Himeraeans to join in the war, and not only to come with them themselves but also to provide arms for the seamen from their vessels, which they had drawn ashore at Himera. They also sent and appointed a place for the Selinuntines to meet them with all their forces. A few troops were also promised by the Geloans and some of the Sicels, who were now ready to join with much greater alacrity, owing to the recent death of Archonidas, a powerful Sicel king in that area who had been friendly to Athens, and also owing to the energy shown by Gylippus in coming from Lacedaemon. Gylippus now took with him about seven hundred of his sailors and marines — only that number having arms — a thousand heavy infantry and light troops from Himera with a force of a hundred horse, some light troops and cavalry from Selinus, a few Geloans, and Sicels numbering a thousand in all, and set out on his march for Syracuse.

Meanwhile the Corinthian fleet from Leucas hurried to arrive. One of their commanders, Gongylus, starting last with a single ship, was the first to reach Syracuse, a little before Gylippus. Gongylus found the Syracusans on the point of holding an assembly to consider whether they should put an end to the war. He prevented this and reassured them by telling them that more vessels were still on the way, and that Gylippus, son of Cleandridas, had been dispatched by the Lacedaemonians to take command. At this the Syracusans took courage, and immediately marched out with all their forces to meet Gylippus, who they found was now close at hand. Meanwhile Gylippus, after taking Ietae, a fort of the Sicels, on his way, formed his army in order of battle, and so arrived at Epipolae. Going up by Euryelus, as the Athenians had done at first, he now advanced with the Syracusans against the Athenian lines. His arrival happened at a critical moment. The Athenians had already finished a double wall of six or seven furlongs to the great harbor, except for a small portion next to the sea, which they were still working on. In the rest of the circle towards Trogilus on the other sea, stones had been laid ready for building for most of the distance, and some points had been left half finished, while others were entirely complete. The danger to Syracuse had indeed been great.

Meanwhile the Athenians, recovering from the confusion into which they had been thrown by the sudden approach of Gylippus and the Syracusans, formed in order of battle. Gylippus halted at a short distance and sent on a herald to tell them that, if they would evacuate Sicily with bag and baggage within five days, he was willing to make a truce on those terms. The Athenians treated this with contempt and dismissed the herald without an answer. Both sides then began to prepare for action. Gylippus, observing that the Syracusans were in disorder and did not easily fall into line, drew off his troops more into the open ground, while Nicias did not lead the Athenians out but lay still by his own wall. When Gylippus saw that they did not come on, he led off his army to the citadel of the quarter of Apollo Temenites and passed the night there. The next day he led out the main body of his army and, drawing them up in order of battle before the walls of the Athenians to keep them from going to the relief of any other quarter, sent a strong force against Fort Labdalum. He took it and put to the sword everyone he found inside, the place not being within sight of the Athenians. On the same day an Athenian galley moored off the harbor was captured by the Syracusans.

After this the Syracusans and their allies began to carry a single wall, starting from the city, slanting up Epipolae, in order that the Athenians, unless they could stop the work, would no longer be able to invest them. Meanwhile the Athenians, having now finished their wall down to the sea, had come up to the heights. Part of their wall being weak, Gylippus drew out his army by night and attacked it. The Athenians who happened to be bivouacking outside took the alarm and came out to meet him, and seeing this he quickly led his men back. The Athenians now built their wall higher, and in future kept guard at this point themselves, posting their confederates along the rest of the works at the stations assigned to them. Nicias also decided to fortify Plemmyrium, a promontory across from the city, which juts out and narrows the mouth of the Great Harbor. He thought that fortifying this place would make it easier to bring in supplies, since they would be able to maintain their blockade from a shorter distance, near the port held by the Syracusans, instead of being obliged, at every movement of the enemy's navy, to put out against them from the bottom of the great harbor. Beyond this, he now began to pay more attention to the war by sea, seeing that the arrival of Gylippus had reduced their hopes by land. So he conveyed across his ships and some troops, built three forts in which he placed most of his baggage, and from then on moored the larger craft and warships there. This was the first and chief cause of the losses the crews experienced. Water was scarce and had to be fetched from far away, and the sailors could not go out for firewood without being cut off by the Syracusan horse, who were masters of the country. A third of the enemy's cavalry was stationed at the little town of Olympieum to prevent plundering raids by the Athenians at Plemmyrium. Meanwhile Nicias learned that the rest of the Corinthian fleet was approaching, and sent twenty ships to watch for them, with orders to be on the lookout for them around Locris and Rhegium and the approaches to Sicily.

Gylippus meanwhile went on with the wall across Epipolae, using the stones the Athenians had laid down for their own wall, and at the same time constantly led out the Syracusans and their allies and formed them in order of battle in front of the lines, the Athenians forming up against him. At last he thought the moment had come and began the attack. A hand-to-hand fight broke out between the lines, where the Syracusan cavalry could be of no use, and the Syracusans and their allies were defeated and took up their dead under truce, while the Athenians erected a trophy. After this Gylippus called the soldiers together and said the fault was not theirs but his: he had kept their lines too far inside the works, and had thus deprived them of the services of their cavalry and javelin-throwers. He would now lead them on a second time. He begged them to remember that in material force they were fully a match for their opponents, and that as for moral advantages, it would be intolerable if Peloponnesians and Dorians could not feel confident of overcoming Ionians, islanders, and the motley rabble that came with them, and of driving them out of the country.

After this he took the first opportunity that offered to lead them against the enemy again. Now Nicias and the Athenians held the view that even if the Syracusans should not wish to offer battle, it was necessary to prevent the building of the cross wall, since it already almost overlapped the extreme point of their own. If it went any further, it would from that moment make no difference whether they fought any number of successful actions or never fought at all. They accordingly came out to meet the Syracusans. Gylippus led out his heavy infantry further from the fortifications than before, and so joined battle, posting his horse and javelin-men on the flank of the Athenians in the open space where the works of the two walls ended. During the engagement the cavalry attacked and routed the left wing of the Athenians, which was opposed to them, and the rest of the Athenian army was in consequence defeated by the Syracusans and driven headlong inside their lines. The night following, the Syracusans carried their wall up to the Athenian works and past them, thus putting it out of the Athenians' power to stop them any longer, and depriving them, even if victorious in the field, of any chance of investing the city in future.

After this the remaining twelve vessels of the Corinthians, Ambraciots, and Leucadians sailed into the harbor under the command of Erasinides, a Corinthian, having eluded the Athenian ships on guard, and helped the Syracusans to complete the rest of the cross wall. Meanwhile Gylippus went into the rest of Sicily to raise land and naval forces, and also to bring over any of the cities that had been lukewarm in the cause or had so far stayed out of the war altogether. Syracusan and Corinthian envoys were also sent to Lacedaemon and Corinth to get a fresh force sent over in any way possible — in merchant vessels or transports, or in any other manner likely to succeed — since the Athenians too were sending for reinforcements. Meanwhile the Syracusans set about manning a fleet and exercising it, intending to try their fortune in this way as well, and generally grew exceedingly confident.

Nicias, seeing this, and seeing the enemy's strength and his own difficulties growing daily, himself also sent word to Athens. He had previously sent frequent reports of events as they occurred, and now he felt it especially incumbent upon him to do so, since he thought they were in a critical position and that, unless speedily recalled or strongly reinforced from home, they had no hope of safety. He feared, however, that the messengers might fail to report the truth — whether through inability to speak, or failure of memory, or a wish to please the multitude — and so thought it best to write a letter, to ensure that the Athenians should know his own opinion without its being lost in transmission, and be able to decide on the real facts of the case.

His emissaries accordingly set out with the letter and the necessary verbal instructions, and he attended to the affairs of the army, making it his aim now to keep on the defensive and avoid any unnecessary danger.

At the close of the same summer the Athenian general Euetion marched in concert with Perdiccas, with a large body of Thracians, against Amphipolis. Failing to take it, he brought some galleys round into the Strymon and blockaded the town from the river, with his base at Himeraeum.

Summer was now over. In the following winter the men sent by Nicias reached Athens, gave the verbal messages they had been entrusted with, answered any questions put to them, and delivered the letter. The clerk of the city then came forward and read it out to the Athenians. It ran as follows:

"Our past operations, Athenians, have been made known to you by many other letters. It is now time for you to become equally familiar with our present condition and to take your measures accordingly. We had defeated the Syracusans, against whom we were sent, in most of our engagements with them, and we had built the works we now hold, when Gylippus arrived from Lacedaemon with an army drawn from the Peloponnese and from some of the cities in Sicily. In our first battle with him we were victorious. In the battle the next day we were overpowered by a multitude of cavalry and javelin-men, and forced to retire within our lines. We have now, therefore, been forced by the numbers opposed to us to halt the work of circumvallation, and to remain inactive — unable to make use even of all the force we have, since a large portion of our heavy infantry is absorbed in defending our lines. Meanwhile the enemy has carried a single wall past our lines, making it impossible for us to invest them in future, unless this cross wall is attacked by a strong force and taken. So the besieger in name has become, at least on the land side, the besieged in reality, since we are prevented by their cavalry from going any distance into the country.

"Besides this, an embassy has been sent to the Peloponnese to procure reinforcements, and Gylippus has gone to the cities in Sicily, partly in the hope of inducing those that are at present neutral to join him in the war, partly to bring from his allies additional contingents for the land forces and materials for the navy. For I understand that they intend a combined attack on our lines with their land forces and with their fleet by sea. None of you should be surprised that I say by sea also. They have discovered that the length of time we have been in commission has rotted our ships and worn out our crews, and that with the wholeness of our crews and the soundness of our ships gone, the original efficiency of our navy has gone with them. It is impossible for us to haul our ships ashore and careen them, because, the enemy's vessels being as many or more than our own, we are constantly expecting an attack. Indeed, they can be seen exercising, and the initiative lies with them. Not having to maintain a blockade, they have greater facilities for drying their ships.

"This we should scarcely be able to do, even if we had plenty of spare ships and were freed from our present need to exhaust all our strength on the blockade. For it is already difficult to bring in supplies past Syracuse, and were we to relax our vigilance in the slightest it would become impossible. The losses our crews have suffered and continue to suffer arise from the following causes. Expeditions for fuel and forage, and the distance from which water has to be fetched, cause our sailors to be cut off by the Syracusan cavalry. The loss of our former superiority emboldens our slaves to desert. Our foreign seamen are intimidated by the unexpected appearance of a navy against us and the strength of the enemy's resistance. Those of them who were pressed into service take the first opportunity to depart to their own cities. Those who were originally tempted in by high pay, expecting little fighting and large profits, leave us either by deserting to the enemy or by taking advantage of one of the many means of escape that the size of Sicily affords. Some even engage in trade themselves and persuade the captains to take Hyccaric slaves on board in their place. In this way they have ruined the efficiency of our navy.

"Now I need not remind you that the time during which a crew is in its prime is short, and that the number of sailors who can start a ship on her way and keep the rowing in time is small. But by far my greatest trouble is that, holding the post that I do, I am prevented by the natural indocility of the Athenian seaman from putting a stop to these evils, and that meanwhile we have no source from which to recruit our crews — something the enemy can do from many quarters — but are compelled to depend, both for supplying the crews in service and for making good our losses, on the men we brought with us. For our present confederates, Naxos and Catana, cannot supply us. There is only one thing more our opponents need: the defection of our Italian markets. If they were to see you neglect to relieve us from our present condition, and were to go over to the enemy, famine would compel us to evacuate, and Syracuse would finish the war without a blow.

"It is true I might have written you something different, more agreeable than this, but nothing certainly more useful, if it is desirable for you to know the real state of things here before taking your measures. Besides, I know it is your nature to love to be told the best side of things, and then to blame the messenger if the expectations he has raised in your minds are not borne out by the result. So I thought it safest to tell you the truth.

"Now you are not to think that either your generals or your soldiers have ceased to be a match for the forces originally opposed to them. But you are to consider that a general Sicilian coalition is forming against us; that a fresh army is expected from the Peloponnese; while the force we have here is unable to cope even with our present opponents. You must promptly decide either to recall us, or to send out to us another fleet and army as numerous again, with a large sum of money, and someone to succeed me, since a disease of the kidneys makes me unfit to retain my post. I have, I think, some claim on your indulgence, since while I was in my prime I did you much good service in my commands. But whatever you mean to do, do it at the start of spring and without delay. The enemy will get his Sicilian reinforcements shortly, and those from the Peloponnese after a longer interval. Unless you attend to the matter, the former will be here before you, while the latter will elude you, as they have done before."

Such were the contents of Nicias's letter. When the Athenians had heard it, they refused to accept his resignation, but chose him two colleagues, naming Menander and Euthydemus, two of the officers at the seat of war, to fill those places until their replacements arrived, so that Nicias would not be left alone in his sickness to bear the whole weight of affairs. They also voted to send out another army and navy, drawn partly from the Athenians on the muster-roll, partly from the allies. The colleagues chosen for Nicias were Demosthenes, son of Alcisthenes, and Eurymedon, son of Thucles. Eurymedon was sent off at once, about the time of the winter solstice, with ten ships, a hundred and twenty talents of silver, and instructions to tell the army that reinforcements would arrive and that they would be looked after. Demosthenes stayed behind to organize the expedition, intending to start as soon as it was spring, and sent for troops from the allies, while meanwhile gathering money, ships, and heavy infantry at home.

The Athenians also sent twenty vessels round the Peloponnese to prevent anyone crossing over to Sicily from Corinth or the Peloponnese. For the Corinthians, filled with confidence by the favorable change in Sicilian affairs reported by the envoys on their arrival, and convinced that the fleet they had sent out before had not been useless, were now preparing to dispatch a force of heavy infantry in merchant vessels to Sicily, while the Lacedaemonians did the same for the rest of the Peloponnese. The Corinthians also manned a fleet of twenty-five vessels, intending to test the result of a battle with the squadron on guard at Naupactus, and meanwhile to make it less easy for the Athenians there to hinder the departure of their merchantmen, by forcing them to keep an eye on the galleys arrayed against them.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians prepared for their invasion of Attica, in accordance with their own previous resolve and at the urging of the Syracusans and Corinthians, who wanted an invasion to halt the reinforcements they had heard Athens was about to send to Sicily. Alcibiades also urgently advised fortifying Decelea and prosecuting the war vigorously. But what most encouraged the Lacedaemonians was the belief that Athens, with two wars on her hands — against themselves and against the Siceliots — would be easier to subdue, and the conviction that she had been the first to violate the truce. In the former war, they considered, the offence had been more on their own side, both because of the Theban entry into Plataea in time of peace, and because of their own refusal to listen to the Athenian offer of arbitration, in spite of the clause in the previous treaty that, where arbitration was offered, there should be no recourse to arms. For this reason they thought they had deserved their misfortunes, and they took to heart the disaster at Pylos and whatever else had befallen them. But when, in addition to the ravages from Pylos, which went on without intermission, the thirty Athenian ships came out from Argos and laid waste part of Epidaurus, Prasiae, and other places; and when, on every dispute that arose about the interpretation of any doubtful point of the treaty, their own offers of arbitration were always rejected by the Athenians; the Lacedaemonians at length decided that Athens had now committed the very same offence as they had committed before, and had become the guilty party. They began to be full of ardor for the war. They spent this winter sending round to their allies for iron and getting ready the other implements for building their fort, and meanwhile began raising at home, and also by forced requisitions in the rest of the Peloponnese, a force to be sent in the merchant vessels to their allies in Sicily. So winter ended, and with it the eighteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

In the first days of the following spring, earlier than usual, the Lacedaemonians and their allies invaded Attica, under the command of Agis, son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians. They began by ravaging the parts bordering on the plain, and then proceeded to fortify Decelea, dividing the work among the various cities. Decelea is about thirteen or fourteen miles from the city of Athens, and the same distance, or not much further, from Boeotia. The fort was meant to harass the plain and the richest parts of the country, and was in sight of Athens. While the Peloponnesians and their allies in Attica were engaged in the work of fortification, their countrymen at home sent off, at about the same time, the heavy infantry in the merchant vessels to Sicily. The Lacedaemonians furnished a picked force of Helots and Neodamodes (or freedmen), six hundred heavy infantry in all, under the command of Eccritus, a Spartan; the Boeotians, three hundred heavy infantry, commanded by two Thebans, Xenon and Nicon, and by Hegesander, a Thespian. These were among the first to put out into the open sea, starting from Taenarus in Laconia. Not long after their departure the Corinthians sent off a force of five hundred heavy infantry, made up partly of men from Corinth itself and partly of Arcadian mercenaries, under the command of Alexarchus, a Corinthian. The Sicyonians also sent off two hundred heavy infantry at the same time as the Corinthians, under the command of Sargeus, a Sicyonian. Meanwhile the twenty-five vessels manned by Corinth during the winter lay confronting the twenty Athenian ships at Naupactus until the heavy infantry in the merchantmen were fairly on their way from the Peloponnese — thus fulfilling the original aim for which they had been manned, which was to divert Athenian attention from the merchant ships to the galleys.

During this time the Athenians were not idle. At the very start of spring, simultaneously with the fortification of Decelea, they sent thirty ships round the Peloponnese, under Charicles, son of Apollodorus, with instructions to call at Argos and demand a force of Argive heavy infantry for the fleet, in keeping with the alliance. At the same time they dispatched Demosthenes to Sicily, as they had intended, with sixty Athenian and five Chian vessels, twelve hundred Athenian heavy infantry from the muster-roll, as many of the islanders as could be raised in the various quarters, and drawing on their other subject allies for whatever they could supply that would be useful for the war. Demosthenes was instructed first to sail round with Charicles and to operate with him on the coasts of Laconia. He accordingly sailed to Aegina and there waited for the rest of his armament, and for Charicles to fetch the Argive troops.

In Sicily, about the same time in this spring, Gylippus came to Syracuse with as many troops as he could bring from the cities he had persuaded to join. Calling the Syracusans together, he told them they must man as many ships as possible and try their hand at a sea-fight, by which he hoped to gain an advantage in the war not unworthy of the risk. With him Hermocrates actively joined in encouraging his countrymen to attack the Athenians at sea, saying that the Athenians had not inherited their naval prowess, nor would they retain it forever. They had been even more landsmen than the Syracusans, and had only become a maritime power when forced to by the Mede. Besides, to daring spirits like the Athenians, a daring adversary would seem the most formidable, and the Athenian plan of paralyzing by the boldness of their attack a neighbor often not their inferior in strength could now be used against them with as good effect by the Syracusans. He was also convinced that the unexpected sight of Syracusans daring to face the Athenian navy would cause a terror in the enemy, the advantages of which would far outweigh any loss that Athenian science might inflict on their inexperience. He accordingly urged them to throw aside their fears and try their fortune at sea. The Syracusans, under the influence of Gylippus, Hermocrates, and perhaps some others, made up their minds for the sea-fight and began to man their ships.

When the fleet was ready, Gylippus led out the whole army by night. His plan was to assault in person the forts on Plemmyrium by land, while thirty-five Syracusan galleys sailed, by appointment, against the enemy from the great harbor, and the forty-five remaining came round from the lesser harbor, where they had their arsenal, in order to join the others inside, and simultaneously to attack Plemmyrium, thus distracting the Athenians by attacking them on two sides at once. The Athenians quickly manned sixty ships, and with twenty-five of these engaged the thirty-five Syracusan ships in the great harbor, sending the rest to meet those sailing round from the arsenal. An action now ensued directly in front of the mouth of the great harbor, kept up with equal tenacity on both sides — the one side wishing to force the passage, the other to prevent them.

In the meantime, while the Athenians at Plemmyrium were down by the sea, attending to the engagement, Gylippus made a sudden attack on the forts in the early morning. He took the largest first, then the two smaller, whose garrisons did not wait for him, seeing the largest taken so easily. At the fall of the first fort, the men from it who managed to take refuge in their boats and merchantmen had great difficulty reaching the camp, since the Syracusans were getting the better of it in the engagement in the great harbor and sent a fast-sailing galley to pursue them. But when the two others fell, the Syracusans were now being defeated, and the fugitives from these sailed alongshore with greater ease. The Syracusan ships fighting off the mouth of the harbor forced their way through the Athenian vessels, but, sailing in without any order, fouled one another and handed victory to the Athenians, who not only routed the squadron in question but also the one by which they had at first been defeated in the harbor, sinking eleven Syracusan vessels and killing most of the men, except the crews of three ships whom they took prisoner. Their own losses were limited to three vessels. After hauling the Syracusan wrecks ashore and setting up a trophy on the islet in front of Plemmyrium, they retired to their own camp.

Unsuccessful at sea, the Syracusans nevertheless held the forts at Plemmyrium, for which they set up three trophies. One of the two later forts they razed; the other two they put in order and garrisoned. In the capture of the forts a great many men were killed and taken prisoner, and a great quantity of property was taken in all. As the Athenians had used them as a magazine, there was a large stock of goods and corn belonging to the merchants inside, and also a large stock belonging to the captains. The masts and other gear of forty galleys were taken, besides three galleys that had been drawn up on shore. Indeed the first and chief cause of the ruin of the Athenian army was the capture of Plemmyrium. Even the entrance of the harbor was now no longer safe for bringing in provisions, since the Syracusan vessels were stationed there to prevent it, and nothing could be brought in without fighting. On top of that there was the general impression of dismay and discouragement produced on the army.

After this the Syracusans sent out twelve ships under the command of Agatharchus, a Syracusan. One of these went to the Peloponnese with ambassadors to describe the hopeful state of their affairs and to urge the Peloponnesians to prosecute the war there even more actively than they were now doing, while the eleven others sailed to Italy, hearing that vessels laden with stores were on their way to the Athenians. After falling in with and destroying most of the vessels in question, and burning in Caulonian territory a quantity of timber for shipbuilding that had been gotten ready for the Athenians, the Syracusan squadron went to Locri. While they were at anchor there, one of the merchantmen from the Peloponnese came in carrying Thespian heavy infantry. They took these on board and sailed alongshore towards home. The Athenians were on the lookout for them with twenty ships at Megara, but were only able to take one vessel with its crew, the rest getting clear off to Syracuse. There was also some skirmishing in the harbor over the piles the Syracusans had driven into the sea in front of the old docks, to allow their ships to lie at anchor inside without being damaged by the Athenians sailing up and ramming them. The Athenians brought up against them a ship of ten thousand talents' burden, fitted with wooden turrets and screens, and from their boats fastened ropes round the piles, wrenched them up and broke them, or dived down and sawed them in two. Meanwhile the Syracusans plied them with missiles from the docks, to which they replied from their large vessel, until at last most of the piles had been removed by the Athenians. But the most awkward part of the stockade was the part out of sight: some of the piles that had been driven in did not appear above water, so it was dangerous to sail up for fear of running the ships onto them, just as on a reef, by not seeing them. Even so, divers went down and sawed off these as well for a reward, although the Syracusans drove in others. Indeed there was no end to the contrivances they resorted to against each other, as might be expected between two hostile armies confronting each other at such close range. Skirmishes and all kinds of other attempts went on constantly. Meanwhile the Syracusans sent embassies to the cities, made up of Corinthians, Ambraciots, and Lacedaemonians, to tell them of the capture of Plemmyrium, and that their defeat in the sea-fight had been due less to the strength of the enemy than to their own disorder. They also wanted to let them know that they were full of hope, and to ask them to come to their help with ships and troops, since the Athenians were expected with a fresh army, and if the one already there could be destroyed before the other arrived, the war would be at an end.

While the contending parties in Sicily were thus engaged, Demosthenes, having now got together the armament with which he was to go to the island, put out from Aegina and, sailing for the Peloponnese, joined Charicles and the thirty Athenian ships. Taking on board the heavy infantry from Argos, they sailed to Laconia, and after first plundering part of Epidaurus Limera, landed on the coast of Laconia, opposite Cythera, where the temple of Apollo stands. Laying waste part of the country, they fortified a kind of isthmus, where the Helots of the Lacedaemonians could desert to, and from which plundering raids could be made as from Pylos. Demosthenes helped to occupy this place, and then immediately sailed on to Corcyra to take up some of the allies on that island, and so to proceed without delay to Sicily. Charicles waited until the fortification of the place was complete and, leaving a garrison there, returned home with his thirty ships and the Argives as well.

This same summer thirteen hundred targeteers — Thracian swordsmen of the tribe of the Dii — arrived at Athens. They were to have sailed to Sicily with Demosthenes, but having come too late, the Athenians decided to send them back to Thrace, where they had come from. Keeping them on for the Decelean war seemed too expensive, the pay of each man being a drachma a day. Indeed, ever since Decelea had been first fortified by the whole Peloponnesian army during this summer, and then occupied to harass the country by garrisons from the cities relieving each other at fixed intervals, it had been doing the Athenians great mischief. In fact this occupation, by the destruction of property and the loss of men it caused, was one of the principal causes of their ruin. Previously the invasions had been short and had not prevented their enjoying their land during the rest of the time. The enemy was now permanently fixed in Attica. Sometimes it was an attack in force, sometimes it was the regular garrison overrunning the country and making forays for its subsistence. The Lacedaemonian king, Agis, was in the field and diligently prosecuting the war. Great mischief was therefore done to the Athenians. They were deprived of their whole country. More than twenty thousand slaves had deserted, a great part of them artisans, and all their sheep and beasts of burden were lost. As the cavalry rode out daily on excursions to Decelea and to guard the country, their horses were either lamed by being constantly worked over rocky ground or wounded by the enemy.

Besides this, the transport of provisions from Euboea, which had previously been carried on far more quickly overland by Decelea from Oropus, was now done at great cost by sea round Sunium. Everything the city required had to be imported from abroad, and instead of a city it became a fortress. Summer and winter the Athenians were worn out by having to keep guard on the fortifications, by day in turns and by night all together, except the cavalry, at the various military posts or on the wall. But what most oppressed them was that they had two wars at once, and had thus reached a pitch of frenzy that no one would have believed possible if he had heard of it before it came to pass. For who could have imagined that, even when besieged by the Peloponnesians entrenched in Attica, they would still, instead of withdrawing from Sicily, stay on there besieging in like manner Syracuse — a town in no way inferior, taken as a town, to Athens? Or that they would so thoroughly upset the Hellenic estimate of their strength and audacity, as to give the spectacle of a people which, at the start of the war, some thought might hold out one year, some two, and none more than three, if the Peloponnesians invaded their country, now seventeen years after the first invasion, after having already suffered every evil of war, going to Sicily and undertaking a new war no less great than the one they already had with the Peloponnesians? These causes — the great losses from Decelea, and the other heavy expenses that fell on them — produced their financial difficulties. It was at this time that they imposed on their subjects, instead of the tribute, a tax of a twentieth on all imports and exports by sea, which they thought would bring them in more money. Their expenditure was now not the same as at first, but had grown with the war, while their revenues had decayed.

Accordingly, not wishing to incur expense in their present shortage of money, they sent back at once the Thracians who had come too late for Demosthenes, under the leadership of Diitrephes. He was instructed, since they were to pass through the Euripus, to use them, if possible, on the voyage along the coast to harm the enemy. Diitrephes first landed them at Tanagra and hastily snatched some plunder. Then he sailed across the Euripus in the evening from Chalcis in Euboea, disembarked in Boeotia, and led them against Mycalessus. The night he passed unobserved near the temple of Hermes, not quite two miles from Mycalessus, and at daybreak he assaulted and took the town, which is not a large one. The inhabitants were off their guard and did not expect that anyone would ever come up so far from the sea to molest them. The wall too was weak, and in some places had tumbled down, while in others it had not been built to any height; the gates also had been left open through their feeling of security. The Thracians bursting into Mycalessus sacked the houses and temples and butchered the inhabitants, sparing neither youth nor age, but killing all they fell in with, one after the other — children and women, even beasts of burden, and whatever other living creatures they saw. The Thracian race, like the bloodiest of the barbarians, is even more bloody when it has nothing to fear. Everywhere there was confusion, and death in all its shapes. In particular they attacked a boys' school, the largest in the place, into which the children had just gone, and massacred them all. In short, the disaster that fell on the whole town was unsurpassed in scale, and unmatched in suddenness and horror.

Meanwhile the Thebans heard of it and marched to the rescue, overtaking the Thracians before they had gone far. They recovered the plunder and drove them in panic to the Euripus and the sea, where the vessels that had brought them were lying. The greatest slaughter took place while they were embarking, since they did not know how to swim, and those in the vessels, on seeing what was happening on shore, moored them out of bowshot. In the rest of the retreat the Thracians made a respectable defense against the Theban horse, by which they were first attacked, dashing out and closing their ranks according to the tactics of their country, and lost only a few men in that part of the affair. A good number who were after plunder were actually caught in the town and put to death. Altogether the Thracians had two hundred and fifty killed out of thirteen hundred. The Thebans and the rest who came to the rescue lost about twenty, troopers and heavy infantry, with Scirphondas, one of the Boeotarchs. The Mycalessians lost a large proportion of their population.

While Mycalessus thus suffered a calamity for its size as lamentable as any that occurred in the war, Demosthenes, whom we left sailing to Corcyra after the building of the fort in Laconia, found a merchantman lying at Phea in Elis, in which the Corinthian heavy infantry were to cross to Sicily. He destroyed the ship, but the men escaped, and afterwards got another in which they continued their voyage. After this, on arriving at Zacynthus and Cephallenia, he took a body of heavy infantry on board, and sending for some of the Messenians from Naupactus, crossed over to the opposite coast of Acarnania, to Alyzia, and to Anactorium, which was held by the Athenians. While he was in these parts he was met by Eurymedon, returning from Sicily, where he had been sent, as has been mentioned, during the winter, with the money for the army. Eurymedon told him the news, including that he had heard, while at sea, that the Syracusans had taken Plemmyrium. Conon also came to them here — the commander at Naupactus — with news that the twenty-five Corinthian ships stationed opposite him, far from giving up the war, were planning an engagement. He therefore begged them to send him some ships, since his own eighteen were not a match for the enemy's twenty-five. Demosthenes and Eurymedon accordingly sent ten of their best sailers with Conon to reinforce the squadron at Naupactus, and meanwhile prepared for the muster of their forces. Eurymedon, who was now Demosthenes' colleague and had turned back as a result of his appointment, sailed to Corcyra to tell them to man fifteen ships and enlist heavy infantry, while Demosthenes raised slingers and javelin-men from the parts about Acarnania.

Meanwhile the envoys mentioned earlier, who had gone from Syracuse to the cities after the capture of Plemmyrium, had succeeded in their mission and were about to bring the army they had collected, when Nicias got wind of it and sent to the Centoripae and Alicyaeans and other friendly Sicels who held the passes, telling them not to let the enemy through but to combine to prevent their passing. There was no other route by which the enemy could even attempt it, since the Agrigentines would not give them passage through their country. In response to this request the Sicels laid a triple ambush for the Siceliots on their march, and attacking them suddenly, while off their guard, killed about eight hundred of them, including all the envoys except the Corinthian, who conducted fifteen hundred who escaped to Syracuse.

About the same time the Camarinaeans also came to the assistance of Syracuse with five hundred heavy infantry, three hundred javelin-men, and as many archers, while the Geloans sent crews for five ships, four hundred javelin-men, and two hundred horse. Indeed almost the whole of Sicily, except the Agrigentines, who were neutral, now ceased merely to watch events as it had been doing, and actively joined Syracuse against the Athenians.

While the Syracusans, after the Sicel disaster, put off any immediate attack on the Athenians, Demosthenes and Eurymedon, whose forces from Corcyra and the continent were now ready, crossed the Ionian Gulf with all their armament to the Iapygian promontory. Starting from there they touched at the Choerades Isles off Iapygia, where they took on board a hundred and fifty Iapygian javelin-men of the Messapian tribe. After renewing an old friendship with Artas the chief, who had supplied them with the javelin-men, they arrived at Metapontium in Italy. Here they persuaded their allies the Metapontines to send three hundred javelin-men and two galleys with them, and with this reinforcement coasted on to Thurii, where they found the party hostile to Athens recently expelled by a revolution. They accordingly stayed there to muster and review the whole army, to see if any had been left behind, and to persuade the Thurians firmly to join them in their expedition, and given the circumstances, to conclude a defensive and offensive alliance with the Athenians.

About the same time the Peloponnesians in the twenty-five ships stationed opposite the squadron at Naupactus to protect the passage of the transports to Sicily had got ready to engage. Manning some additional vessels so as to be numerically little inferior to the Athenians, they anchored off Erineus in Achaia in the Rhypic country. The place where they lay was in the form of a crescent. The land forces furnished by the Corinthians and their allies on the spot came up and ranged themselves on the projecting headlands on either side, while the fleet, under the command of Polyanthes, a Corinthian, held the intervening space and blocked up the entrance. The Athenians under Diphilus now sailed out against them with thirty-three ships from Naupactus. The Corinthians at first did not move, but at length thought they saw their opportunity, raised the signal, and advanced and engaged the Athenians. After a stubborn struggle, the Corinthians lost three ships, and without sinking any altogether, disabled seven of the enemy, which were struck prow to prow and had their forequarters stove in by the Corinthian vessels, whose cheeks had been strengthened for this very purpose. After an engagement of this even character — in which either party could claim the victory, although the Athenians became masters of the wrecks because the wind drove them out to sea, the Corinthians not putting out again to meet them — the two sides parted. There was no pursuit, and no prisoners taken on either side. The Corinthians and Peloponnesians fighting near the shore escaped easily, and none of the Athenian vessels was sunk. The Athenians now sailed back to Naupactus, and the Corinthians at once set up a trophy as victors, on the grounds that they had disabled a greater number of the enemy's ships. They held that they had not been worsted, for the very same reason their opponents held they had not been victorious — the Corinthians considering they were conquerors if not decidedly conquered, and the Athenians thinking themselves vanquished because not decidedly victorious. However, when the Peloponnesians sailed off and their land forces had dispersed, the Athenians also set up a trophy as victors in Achaia, about two and a quarter miles from Erineus, the Corinthian station.

This was the end of the action at Naupactus. To return to Demosthenes and Eurymedon: the Thurians having now got ready to join in the expedition with seven hundred heavy infantry and three hundred javelin-men, the two generals ordered the ships to sail along the coast to Crotonian territory, and meanwhile held a review of all the land forces on the river Sybaris, and then led them through the Thurian country. On reaching the river Hylias they received a message from the Crotonians that they would not allow the army to pass through their country, at which the Athenians descended toward the shore and bivouacked near the sea and the mouth of the Hylias, where the fleet also met them. The next day they embarked and sailed along the coast, touching at all the cities except Locri, until they came to Petra in Rhegian territory.

Meanwhile the Syracusans, hearing of their approach, decided to make a second attempt with their fleet and their other forces on shore, which they had been collecting for this very purpose, in order to do something before the Athenians arrived. In addition to other improvements suggested by the previous sea-fight, which they now adopted in the equipment of their navy, they cut down their prows to a smaller compass to make them more solid, and made their cheeks stouter, and from these let stays into the vessels' sides for a length of six cubits within and without — in the same way the Corinthians had altered their prows before engaging the squadron at Naupactus. The Syracusans thought that they would in this way have an advantage over the Athenian vessels, which were not built with equal strength but were slight in the bows, since they were more used to sailing round and charging the enemy's side than to meeting him prow to prow. They also reckoned that the battle being in the great harbor, with a great many ships in not much room, was also in their favor. Charging prow to prow, they would stave in the enemy's bows by striking with solid, stout beaks against hollow, weak ones. Secondly, the Athenians for want of room would be unable to use their favorite maneuver of breaking the line or of sailing round, since the Syracusans would do their best not to let them do the one, and want of room would prevent their doing the other. This charging prow to prow, which had hitherto been considered a sign of unskillful steering, would be the Syracusans' chief maneuver, as the one they would find most useful — for the Athenians, if repulsed, would not be able to back water in any direction except toward the shore, and that only for a short distance, and in the small space in front of their own camp. The rest of the harbor would be commanded by the Syracusans, and the Athenians, if hard pressed, by crowding together into a small space all toward the same point, would run foul of one another and fall into disorder, which was in fact the thing that did the Athenians the most harm in all the sea-fights, since they did not have, like the Syracusans, the whole harbor to retreat over. As for sailing round into the open sea, this would be impossible with the Syracusans in possession of the way out and in, especially since Plemmyrium would be hostile to them, and the mouth of the harbor was not large.

With these contrivances to suit their skill and capacity, and now more confident after the previous sea-fight, the Syracusans attacked by land and sea at once. The town force Gylippus led out a little earlier and brought up to the wall of the Athenians where it faced the city, while the force from the Olympieum — that is, the heavy infantry that were there, with the horse and the light troops of the Syracusans — advanced against the wall from the opposite side. The ships of the Syracusans and allies sailed out immediately afterwards. The Athenians at first imagined they were to be attacked by land only, and it was not without alarm that they saw the fleet suddenly approaching as well. While some were forming up on the walls and in front of them against the advancing enemy, and some marching out in haste against the numbers of horse and javelin-men coming from the Olympieum and from outside, others manned the ships or rushed down to the beach to face the enemy. When the ships were manned, they put out with seventy-five sail against about eighty of the Syracusans.

After spending a great part of the day in advancing, retreating, and skirmishing with each other, without either being able to gain any advantage worth speaking of — except that the Syracusans sank one or two of the Athenian vessels — they parted, the land force at the same time withdrawing from the lines. The next day the Syracusans remained quiet and gave no sign of what they were going to do. But Nicias, seeing that the battle had been a draw and expecting them to attack again, compelled the captains to refit any of the ships that had been damaged, and moored merchant vessels in front of the stockade they had driven into the sea in front of their ships, to serve as a kind of enclosed harbor, at about two hundred feet from each other, so that any ship hard pressed could retreat safely and sail out again at leisure. These preparations occupied the Athenians all day until nightfall.

The next day the Syracusans began operations at an earlier hour, but with the same plan of attack by land and sea. A great part of the day the rivals spent as before, confronting and skirmishing with each other. At last Ariston, son of Pyrrhicus, a Corinthian, the ablest helmsman in Syracusan service, persuaded their naval commanders to send to the officials in the city and tell them to move the sale market as quickly as possible down to the sea, and to oblige everyone to bring whatever eatables he had and sell them there. This would let the commanders land the crews and dine at once close to the ships, and shortly afterward, on the same day, attack the Athenians again when they were not expecting it.

In compliance with this advice a messenger was sent and the market made ready, on which the Syracusans suddenly backed water and withdrew to the town, and at once landed and took their dinner on the spot. The Athenians, supposing they had returned to the town because they felt themselves beaten, disembarked at their leisure and set about getting their dinners and other occupations, under the impression that they were done with fighting for the day. Suddenly the Syracusans had manned their ships and were once again sailing against them. The Athenians, in great confusion and most of them with empty stomachs, got on board, and with great difficulty put out to meet them. For some time both sides remained on the defensive without engaging, until at last the Athenians decided not to let themselves be worn out by waiting where they were, but to attack without delay, and giving a cheer, went into action. The Syracusans received them, and charging prow to prow as they had intended, stove in a great part of the Athenian foreships by the strength of their beaks. The javelin-men on the decks also did great damage to the Athenians, but still greater damage was done by the Syracusans who went about in small boats, ran in upon the oars of the Athenian galleys, sailed against their sides, and from there discharged their javelins at the sailors.

At last, fighting hard in this way, the Syracusans gained the victory, and the Athenians turned and fled between the merchantmen to their own station. The Syracusan ships pursued them as far as the merchantmen, where they were stopped by the beams armed with dolphins suspended from those vessels over the passage. Two of the Syracusan vessels went too near in the excitement of victory and were destroyed, one of them being taken with its crew. After sinking seven of the Athenian vessels and disabling many more, and taking most of the men prisoners and killing others, the Syracusans retired and set up trophies for both the engagements, now confident of having a decided superiority by sea, and by no means despairing of equal success by land.
